say.text: A cancer registry summary lists the most common cancer in women in India first. Which cancer tops it today?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Breast cancer is now the most common cancer in women in India and worldwide.
That is not the right choice.
Cervix is tempting: it was the PYQ answer for years, so it is memorised. But that key is out of date, and the incidence picture has moved on.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so date the fact: a memorised PYQ answer can outlive the data behind it.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Ovarian cancer is a real cancer in women, but the question asks for the top of the list, and it is not there.
Ask when the answer you memorised was written, and whether the incidence data have changed since.
Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in India and worldwide.
Cervix was the answer in older keys, which is why it still comes to mind. Note the date on any PYQ key.
A 50-year-old has a new hard breast lump. Before chemotherapy, the oncology team asks for ER, PR and HER2 status. Which sample do you send?

choices.label: Core needle biopsy of the lump
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A core biopsy shows whether the tumour is invasive and gives grade, ER, PR and HER2 status.
That is not the right choice.
FNAC is the old key answer, and it is quick and cheap, so it feels right. But a few cells cannot show invasion, grade or receptor status.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the pathologist must report before you choose the test.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Excision gives tissue, but it is a surgical step taken before the team has a receptor plan, so it is the wrong first sample.
Ask what the team needs to read on the slide: whether the cancer invades, and what its receptors are.
Core needle biopsy is preferred, because it separates invasive from in situ disease and gives receptor status. FNAC is kept mainly for nodes and cysts.
A surgeon tells you: 'Bloody discharge from one duct is usually cancer, so biopsy every case.' Which version is accurate?

choices.label: Exclude cancer, but the commonest cause is benign
Cancer is the commonest cause, so biopsy all
Not sure, give me a hint
Duct ectasia is commonest, so observe all

say.text: Yes. Bloody discharge must be investigated to exclude cancer, while the commonest cause, intraductal papilloma, is benign.
That is not the right choice.
The fear of cancer is real, so a 'most common' sentence sounds safe. But a red-flag sign is not the same as the commonest cause; keep those two claims apart.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: 'must be excluded' does not mean 'most frequent'.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Duct ectasia is a common cause of discharge, but a bloody sign must be investigated, not observed as a rule.
Separate two questions: how often does each cause occur, and which diagnosis must you never miss?
The commonest cause of bloody discharge is intraductal papilloma, but carcinoma must still be excluded. Frequency and red-flag status are different claims.
A pathologist warns that the tumour may also be present, at several sites, in the other breast. Which histological type makes that most likely?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Lobular cells grow in single file with loss of E-cadherin, so the tumour is often bilateral and multicentric.
That is not the right choice.
NST is the commonest type, so it is the default for any histology question. But frequency does not tell you the pattern of spread.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the stem asks for the commonest type or the one with this pattern.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Medullary is a rarer type with its own features, and it is not the one known for bilateral, multicentric spread.
Ask which type grows as cells in single file, and which type loses E-cadherin.
Invasive lobular carcinoma is the type most often bilateral or multicentric, because its cells lose E-cadherin and grow in single file.
Which BRCA statement is NOT correct?

choices.label: BRCA2 is linked to male breast cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. BRCA1 lies on 17q, so the statement that puts it on 13q is the one that is not correct. BRCA2 is the 13q gene.
That is not the right choice.
The two numbers are easy to swap, so you may hold BRCA2 on 17q in memory. This statement is true, and the question wants the one that is not.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but the two numbers were held as a pair. Anchor each gene to its own arm.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
This statement is true: BRCA2 is the gene more associated with male breast cancer. The question asks for the one that is not correct.
Hold the two arms apart: which gene do you tie to 17, and which to 13?
BRCA1 is on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q. So the statement that puts BRCA1 on 13q is the one that is not correct.
A 58-year-old man has breast cancer, and his sister had ovarian cancer at 45. Which gene should the genetics team test first?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. BRCA2 is the gene more associated with male breast cancer, so it is the first test in a man.
That is not the right choice.
BRCA1 is the famous breast gene, and its tumours are often triple-negative in women, so it is tempting. But this patient is a man, and the male-linked gene is the other one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the patient's sex first, then the gene linked to it.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
PTEN belongs to other inherited syndromes. The breast and ovarian family pattern points to the BRCA pair.
Ask which gene is most linked with male breast cancer, then check the family pattern.
BRCA2 is the gene more associated with male breast cancer, and BRCA1 is the one more often seen in women with triple-negative tumours. In a man, test BRCA2 first.
Under current AJCC staging, which description of ipsilateral supraclavicular node involvement is correct?

choices.label: It makes the disease M1, distant metastasis
A regional N3c category, not distant disease
It is N2b, the internal mammary station
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes stay on the nodal ladder as N3c, so the disease is still regional.
That is not the right choice.
The old classification counted nodes above the clavicle as distant, so M1 feels right. But M1 covers nodes on the other side or distant organs, not this side's nodes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the side and the ladder before you choose the M category.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Internal mammary nodes are a different station on the nodal ladder. They are not the category for supraclavicular disease.
Ask two things: which side is the node on, and where does the N ladder place nodes on that side?
Ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes are N3c. Only contralateral supraclavicular or other distant disease counts as M1.
On a staging sheet, the skin over a tumour looks like orange peel. There is no ulceration, no redness and no warmth. Which T code do you enter?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Peau d'orange is a skin sign that puts the tumour in T4b, and T4d needs the full inflammatory picture.
That is not the right choice.
The orange-peel sign sounds inflammatory, so T4d is tempting. But the sign on its own does not make inflammatory carcinoma.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the whole breast: a skin sign is one finding, while T4d is a picture.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
T4a means extension to ribs, intercostal muscles or serratus anterior, and the sheet records no chest-wall finding.
Ask what the skin sign is, and whether the whole breast shows the inflammatory picture.
Peau d'orange alone is skin involvement, T4b. T4d needs the inflammatory picture: a red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange over at least a third of it.
A 1.8 cm tumour is attached to pectoralis major only. The ribs, intercostal muscles and serratus anterior move freely. What is its T category?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Fixity to pectoralis major alone is not chest-wall disease, and a tumour of 2 cm or less is T1.
That is not the right choice.
The pectoralis sits right beside the tumour, so fixity feels like chest-wall spread. But the T4a list is ribs, intercostals and serratus, not the pectoralis alone.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the chest-wall list again: pectoralis major is not on it.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
T2 needs more than 2 cm, and this tumour is under that size, so size places it in T1.
Ask what the fixity actually touches, and whether that structure is on the T4a list.
Fixity to pectoralis major alone is not T4a. With no chest-wall or skin extension, the tumour is classed by size, and 2 cm or less is T1.
Which statement about Halsted and modified radical mastectomy is correct?

choices.label: Halsted spares the axilla; MRM clears it
MRM spares pectoralis major; Halsted removes it
Halsted is now the standard for operable cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. MRM removes the breast and nodes but keeps pectoralis major, while Halsted also removes the pectoral muscles.
That is not the right choice.
Halsted's wide clearance feels thorough, so it can look like the default. But it is now rarely done, and the operation depends on suitability.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the old standard removed and why current practice changed.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Both operations clear the axilla. What separates them is the pectoral muscle, not the nodes.
Look at the muscles each operation takes, not only the nodes.
Halsted removes the breast, pectoralis major, pectoralis minor and all axillary levels, and is now rarely done. MRM keeps pectoralis major.
Which statement about breast cancer drug heart toxicity is NOT correct?

choices.label: Trastuzumab damage is usually reversible and not dose-related
Trastuzumab damage is dose-dependent and irreversible
Doxorubicin damage is cumulative and dose-dependent
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. That is the false statement: trastuzumab's cardiac effect is usually reversible and not dose-related.
That is not the right choice.

The anthracycline pattern is tempting to copy across, so a reversible, not dose-related statement can look suspicious. But it describes trastuzumab accurately, so it is not the one the question wants.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so do not carry the anthracycline pattern over to other heart-toxic drugs.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
This statement is true: doxorubicin's damage is cumulative and dose-dependent. Keep it as the reference point for the other drug.
Ask which of these drugs behaves like a cumulative anthracycline, and which does not.

Trastuzumab's cardiotoxicity is usually reversible and not dose-related, unlike doxorubicin's cumulative, largely irreversible damage. So the dose-dependent, irreversible statement is the one that is not correct.
A 68-year-old woman, long past her periods, has ER-positive disease. Her oncologist wants a drug that stops oestrogen being made in her body. Which class fits?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint
An aromatase inhibitor, such as letrozole

say.text: Yes. After menopause most oestrogen comes from peripheral aromatisation, so an aromatase inhibitor cuts that source.
That is not the right choice.
ER-positive is the cue, and tamoxifen is the default for it, so it feels right. But tamoxifen blocks the receptor; it does not stop oestrogen being made, and menopausal status decides the drug.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but ER-positive is not enough on its own: check menopausal status before the drug.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Raloxifene is used in chemoprevention in postmenopausal women, not as the usual treatment for this patient.
Ask where this woman's oestrogen comes from after menopause, and what the drug has to stop.
After menopause oestrogen comes mainly from peripheral aromatisation, so an aromatase inhibitor is the usual choice. Tamoxifen is the usual choice for premenopausal women.
A woman on tamoxifen for three years has new postmenopausal bleeding. What should the team do first?

choices.label: Sample the endometrium; tamoxifen raises cancer risk
Reassure her; tamoxifen protects the lining
Not sure, give me a hint
Bone scan; aromatase inhibitors cause bone loss

say.text: Yes. Tamoxifen raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma, so bleeding on it needs sampling before reassurance.
That is not the right choice.
Tamoxifen blocks oestrogen in the breast, so a protective effect on the lining feels logical. But its action differs by tissue, and the uterine effect is a risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that tissue-specific action does not mean protection in every tissue.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Bone loss is a real aromatase-inhibitor problem, but it does not explain new bleeding on tamoxifen.
Ask whether a drug that acts as a blocker in the breast acts the same way on the uterus.
Tamoxifen acts differently in the uterus and raises endometrial cancer risk, so postmenopausal bleeding on it is sampled, not reassured.
A core biopsy shows classic LCIS with no invasive cancer, found on a mammogram. Which plan item is NOT part of the right plan?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Classic LCIS is a risk marker, not a cancer to remove, so mastectomy is not part of this plan.
That is not the right choice.
Surveillance can feel like doing nothing, so it looks wrong for an in-situ lesion. But it is part of the plan for classic LCIS, so it is not the item this question wants.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether this lesion is a precursor to remove or a marker to follow.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Chemoprevention is part of the plan for classic LCIS, so it is not the item this question wants.
Ask what classic LCIS represents: a cancer to remove, or a marker of later risk?
Classic LCIS is a risk marker for invasive cancer in either breast. It is managed with surveillance and chemoprevention, and mastectomy is not part of that plan.
